Mirfield.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Calder Valley
s1loc: Mirfield's marquee draws sit around the River Calder and the Calder and Hebble Navigation, which opened through the town in 1766 and now carries narrowboats past Mirfield Marina. St Mary the Virgin parish church, designed by Sir George Gilbert Scott and completed in 1871, stands beside the medieval tower of its predecessor, while the curious stone Temple and the 26-foot Dumb Steeple column give the West Yorkshire town its own roster of local landmarks.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Ings Grove Park, a green space with a play area, seating and the town Cenotaph, and on the towpath walks that thread the canal and the Calder. Hopton, one of the historic hamlets that make up Mirfield, keeps its own character on the valley side, and the wooded ridges above the river give walkers and day-trippers routes out across the Calder Valley through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run deep through the Community of the Resurrection, the Anglican monastery whose College of the Resurrection trains priests and whose church is open to the public daily. Mirfield is the birthplace of Sir Patrick Stewart, and its old coaching trade is recalled by the Three Nuns, the long-standing inn on the Huddersfield road, while the Bagshaw Museum in its Victorian mansion at nearby Batley adds to the local heritage offer.

The visitor trade leans on a town and country hotel base and a guide scene built around the canal, the College and the Calder Valley. Mirfield station puts the town on the Huddersfield line between Leeds, Wakefield and Manchester, with the A644 and A62 carrying day-trippers on to Dewsbury, Brighouse and Huddersfield, while the moors, mills and reservoirs of the surrounding Kirklees countryside spread a wide seasonal catchment around the town.

Yeadon.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Aireborough
s1loc: Yeadon's best-known landmark is Leeds Bradford Airport, immediately east of the town, where the wartime Avro factory built aircraft from 1938 to 1946 and which today is the visitor gateway for the whole of West Yorkshire. Yeadon Tarn sits beside the runway as a picturesque sailing and birdwatching water, and St John the Evangelist Church of 1844 anchors a town centre that grew on the woollen trade of the Aire Valley above Leeds.

The leisure and activity layer reaches Yeadon Tarn for sailing, model boating and lakeside walks, and out to Otley Chevin and the Chevin Forest Park, the high gritstone ridge between Airedale and Wharfedale whose view over Otley and the Wharfe is famous across Yorkshire. The commons, woods and reservoirs of the surrounding Aireborough countryside give families and walkers room to roam through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture centre on Yeadon Town Hall, the French Gothic building of 1880 by William Hill with its clock tower, Mechanics' Institute roots and 560-seat theatre staging music, comedy, film and drama. The historic townships of Guiseley, Rawdon and Yeadon that once formed Aireborough keep their own identity, and the nearby village of Esholt and Salts Mill at Saltaire in the Aire Valley add to the area's heritage draw.

The visitor trade leans on a hotel base built around the airport and the city and a guide scene linking the Tarn, the Chevin and Wharfedale. Leeds Bradford Airport puts the town on the national and European map, with the A658 and A65 carrying day-trippers between Leeds, Bradford and the Dales, while Otley, Ilkley Moor and the wider Wharfedale countryside spread a broad seasonal catchment around Yeadon.

Peterlee.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Durham Coast
s1loc: Peterlee's marquee draw is the Apollo Pavilion, the striking concrete bridge and public artwork designed by Victor Pasmore over the Sunny Blunts estate, opened in 1969 and now Grade II listed after its Heritage Lottery restoration. Founded as a New Town in 1948 and named after the miners' leader Peter Lee, the County Durham town sits on the coalfield coast and acts as a base for the wider Durham Heritage Coast and its dramatic cliffs and denes.

The leisure and activity layer is led by Castle Eden Dene National Nature Reserve just east of the town, an ancient woodland and Site of Special Scientific Interest crossed by the Squirrel Walk and Yew Tree Walk, with more than 450 plant species, roe deer and fox. Beyond it the denes, beaches and clifftop England Coast Path of Horden and Blackhall give walkers and families room to roam through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run through the coalfield story of the surrounding pit villages of Horden, Shotton and Blackhall and through the area's mining memory, alongside the public art and modernist planning legacy that make Peterlee itself an unusual heritage subject. The nearby town of Seaham and its harbour, with the Tommy soldier sculpture and sea-glass beaches, broadens the local events and visitor calendar along the Durham Coast.

The visitor trade leans on a town and coastal hotel base and a guide scene built around the Dene, the Pavilion and the coast path. The A19 runs past the town linking Sunderland, Hartlepool and Teesside, with rail at Horden putting the Durham Coast Line within reach, while Seaham, Houghton le Spring and the City of Durham spread a wide seasonal catchment of attractions around Peterlee.

Faversham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Kent Swale
s1loc: Faversham's marquee draw is the Shepherd Neame brewery, Britain's oldest brewer, trading in the centre of the town since 1698 with a visitor centre and brewery tours that pull in beer tourists across the year. One of England's oldest market towns, set beside the Swale and Faversham Creek, it holds a thrice-weekly market in the timber-framed Guildhall square and a run of medieval streets that make the whole centre a draw in their own right.

The leisure and activity layer reaches the tidal Faversham Creek and Standard Quay, where Thames sailing barges still moor, and the scenic Stonebridge Pond beneath the Norman Davington Priory. Oare Gunpowder Works Country Park preserves the town's explosives heritage as woodland and water, while Brogdale, home of the National Fruit Collection, offers orchard tours and pick-your-own across 150 acres of countryside just outside the centre through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run through the Fleur de Lis Heritage Centre and Museum in Preston Street, run by the Faversham Society, and the 12th-century thatched Maison Dieu at Ospringe, one of the country's longest-surviving village museums. The Alexander Centre, the medieval parish church of St Mary with its distinctive crown spire and the gunpowder story that armed Trafalgar and Waterloo give the town a deep events and exhibition calendar.

The visitor trade leans on a town and coaching-inn hotel base and a guide scene built around the brewery, the creek and Brogdale. Faversham station puts the town on the high-speed and mainline route to Whitstable, Canterbury, Sittingbourne and London, while the Swale marshes, the Saxon Shore Way and the North Downs spread a wide seasonal catchment of day-trips and walks around the market town.

Burnham-on-Sea.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Somerset coast
s1loc: Burnham-on-Sea's marquee landmark is the Low Lighthouse, the white-and-red 'lighthouse on legs' built in 1832 and standing on nine wooden piers on the sands, one of the most photographed sights on the Somerset coast. The traditional resort runs a wide level Esplanade of amusement arcades, fish-and-chip shops and seafront cafes overlooking the Bristol Channel, with the High Lighthouse on Berrow Road and the old pillar lighthouse completing the town's distinctive trio of beacons.

The leisure and activity layer reaches the vast tidal beaches of Burnham, Berrow and Brean, and Apex Leisure and Wildlife Park, a 42-acre site of lakes, play areas, a skatepark and a BMX track beside the River Brue at Highbridge. Brean Leisure Park and its theme park rides sit just up the coast, while Brean Down, the dramatic limestone promontory with its Victorian fort, juts a mile and a half into the Channel.

Heritage and culture run through the seafront bandstand and the Princess Theatre and Arts Centre on the Esplanade, the BARB and RNLI lifeboat stations whose crews patrol the treacherous Channel sands, and St Andrew's Church with its leaning tower and Augustus Pugin altar screen. The traditional carnival calendar of Burnham and nearby Bridgwater, the donkey rides on the sands and the views to Steep Holm and Flat Holm give the town an old-fashioned seaside character.

The visitor trade leans on a hotel, guesthouse and holiday-park base spread between Burnham, Berrow and Brean and a guide scene built around the beaches and the lighthouses. The M5 at junctions 22 and 23 brings day-trippers in from Bristol and the South West, with the A38 linking Bridgwater and Highbridge, while Weston-super-Mare, Clevedon and the Somerset Levels spread a broad seasonal catchment around the resort.

Northwich.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of mid-Cheshire
s1loc: Northwich's marquee draw is the Anderton Boat Lift, the Victorian 'Cathedral of the Canals' built by Edwin Clark in 1875 to raise boats between the River Weaver and the Trent and Mersey Canal, restored to hydraulic working in 2002 and one of the Seven Wonders of the Waterways, with a visitor centre and boat trips. The mid-Cheshire town grew on salt, and its waterways and half-timbered Black-and-White centre give it a strong sense of place.

The leisure and activity layer is led by Marbury Country Park, the wooded former Marbury Hall estate with lakeside trails, a bird hide and picnic grounds, and by the linked Anderton Nature Park and Carey Park along the Weaver. The flashes, meres and woods of the surrounding Northwich Community Woodlands, formed on old subsidence ground, give walkers, cyclists and families room to roam through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run through the Lion Salt Works, the restored open-pan salt-making museum on the Trent and Mersey Canal that tells the story of Cheshire's 'white gold', and through the timber-framed buildings of the town centre rebuilt after salt-mining subsidence. The Weaver Hall Museum, the riverside quarter and the village of Great Budworth nearby add to a heritage offer that runs across mid-Cheshire's salt and waterway story.

The visitor trade leans on a town and canalside hotel base and a guide scene built around the boat lift, the salt works and the meres. Northwich station links the town to Manchester, Chester and Liverpool, with the A556 and the M6 carrying day-trippers across Cheshire, while Tatton Park, Delamere Forest and the wider Cheshire countryside spread a wide seasonal catchment of attractions around the town.

Bangor.region: Bangor and the North Wales coast
Bangor.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of North West Wales
s1loc: Bangor, the oldest city in Wales and one of the smallest in the UK, sits between the Menai Strait and the foothills of Eryri, its marquee draws led by the Grade II listed Garth Pier, the 470-metre Victorian promenade that is the second longest in Wales and reaches out toward Anglesey. Bangor Cathedral, founded by Saint Deiniol in the 6th century on one of Britain's oldest Christian sites, anchors a city centre rich in history above the strait.

The leisure and activity layer reaches the waterfront and Garth Pier, the slopes of Bangor Mountain above the city and the strait-side walks toward the Menai Suspension Bridge of 1826. Penrhyn Castle, the vast 19th-century country house and grounds in the care of the National Trust just east of the city, draws families across the season, while the mountains, lakes and trails of Eryri and the Anglesey coast lie on the doorstep.

Heritage and culture run through Storiel, the county museum and gallery of Gwynedd beside the cathedral, and through Pontio, the Grimshaw-designed arts centre run by Bangor University with its Bryn Terfel theatre, studio theatre and 200-seat cinema staging film, drama, music and circus. Thomas Telford's Menai Suspension Bridge and Robert Stephenson's Britannia Bridge across the strait add landmark engineering heritage to the city's draw.

The visitor trade leans on a city and university hotel base and a guide scene built around the pier, the cathedral and the mountains. Bangor station puts the city on the North Wales Coast Line between Chester, Holyhead and the Anglesey ferry, with the A55 expressway carrying day-trippers along the coast, while Llandudno, Conwy, Caernarfon and the peaks of Eryri spread a wide seasonal catchment around the city.
